reason: Pioneer 10 offers a rich narrative of groundbreaking 'firsts' and a fascinating alien message with well-documented scientific mysteries.
story: Launched in 1972, Pioneer 10 was a mission of radical 'firsts.' It was the first human-made object to navigate the asteroid belt and the first to reach Jupiter, surviving radiation levels high enough to trigger false commands in its hardware. While its instruments captured the first close-up images of the Great Red Spot, its most famous cargo was a golden message to the stars. Affixed to its exterior is a gold-anodized aluminum plaque designed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake. This 'cosmic receipt' features nude human figures and a pulsar map revealing our exact location in the galaxy. After three decades of operation, the probe sent its final signal from 7.6 billion miles away in 2003. Now, the silent spacecraft drifts toward the star Aldebaran, carrying the story of humanity into the interstellar dark. Even its weirdest mystery—a tiny, unexplained drag known as the Pioneer Anomaly—was eventually traced back to its own escaping heat.
angle: Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to navigate the asteroid belt and reach Jupiter, carrying a golden 'nude' map of Earth that survived radiation 400 times a human's lethal dose.

claims.claim: Pioneer 10 launched on March 3, 1972 (March 2 local time) aboard an Atlas-Centaur rocket.
It was the first spacecraft to travel through the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
The mission was the first to achieve the escape velocity required to leave the Solar System.
Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to fly past Jupiter, reaching closest approach in December 1973.
The spacecraft passed within approximately 132,000 kilometers (82,000 miles) of Jupiter.
Intense Jovian radiation caused the spacecraft to generate false commands, leading to the loss of some images.
The spacecraft returned more than 500 images of Jupiter and its atmosphere.
It carried a 6-by-9-inch gold-anodized aluminum plaque designed as a message for extraterrestrial life.
The plaque was designed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake, with artwork by Linda Salzman Sagan.
The plaque depicts a nude man and woman alongside a map of 14 pulsars to show the Sun's location.
The plaque uses the hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen as a universal unit for time and distance.
Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to use all-nuclear electrical power via radioisotope thermoelectric generators.
In June 1983, it became the first human-made object to pass beyond the orbits of the major planets by crossing Neptune's orbit.
The final signal from the spacecraft was received on January 23, 2003.
Scientists discovered the 'Pioneer Anomaly,' a small, persistent frequency drift in the spacecraft's radio signal.
The anomaly was eventually attributed to the recoil force of uneven heat radiation from the spacecraft.
The spacecraft is currently traveling toward the constellation Taurus and the star Aldebaran.

disputed: The status of Pluto as a planet: Sources from the mission era (S6, S7) describe it as the outermost planet, but later sources (S1, S2) clarify its reclassification as a dwarf planet; the script should note it was 'then considered the outermost planet.'

The cause of the Pioneer Anomaly: Older sources (S5) treat it as a mystery involving dark matter or new physics, while the most recent analysis (S1) confirms it was caused by thermal radiation; the script should attribute the solution to later analysis.

Censorship of the plaque: One source (S2) details controversies regarding the lack of female genitalia and racial representation; the script should attribute these to artistic and administrative compromises if mentioned.
